title: The AI Supply Chain
tagline: From EUV scanner to the AI app on your screen. Every number sourced.

intro.headline: Every AI answer has a supply chain.
intro.text: Two streams make every AI answer. One builds the computers: one-of-a-kind machines print chips, the chips are stacked with special memory, packed into servers and plugged into buildings that draw as much power as a small city. The other gathers what models learn from: text, human feedback and software. The streams meet when a model is trained, and flow on into the apps you use. A few companies at a few steps hold the whole thing together.

compute.name: Compute
compute.text: Building the computers AI runs on

merge.name: The streams meet
merge.text: Compute and data come together to train a model. From here the chain is one stream, all the way to you.

T1.headline: Machines that print chips
T1.text: Chips are made by shining light through a pattern onto silicon. The newest chips need extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light, and only one company in the world builds those machines.

T2.headline: Factories that make the chips
T2.text: Those machines go into fabs, the factories that turn silicon wafers into chips. At the leading edge, almost every AI chip is made by one company, mostly on one island.

T3.headline: Companies that design the chips
T3.text: Nvidia, AMD, Google, Amazon and others design AI chips, but they don't own the factories. They send their designs to the foundries. Nvidia leads, and the big cloud companies are building their own chips to depend on it less.

T4.headline: Memory stacked next to the chip
T4.text: AI chips are hungry for data, so they sit beside towers of stacked memory called HBM. Only three companies make it, and supply is tight.

T5.headline: Packaging: chip and memory become one
T5.text: The chip and its memory are joined on one base so data can move between them fast. This step sounds minor, but it has been one of the biggest bottlenecks in AI hardware.

T6.headline: Servers and the network between them
T6.text: Packaged chips go into servers, and thousands of servers are wired together so they act like one giant computer. The network matters as much as the chips.

T7.headline: Buildings, cooling and power
T7.text: Servers need data centers, liquid cooling and lots of electricity. Today the slowest part of building AI capacity is often getting enough power: transformers, switchgear and a grid connection.

T8.headline: Clouds that rent out the compute
T8.text: Hyperscalers like AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, and newer neoclouds like CoreWeave, own the GPUs and rent them out by the hour to AI labs and companies.

D1.headline: What models learn from
D1.text: A model learns from huge amounts of text, code and images scraped from the web or licensed from publishers, then from people who rate and correct its answers. All of it is processed with a software stack where one piece, Nvidia's CUDA, is as hard to replace as the chips themselves.

T9.headline: Training: where the streams meet
T9.text: AI labs rent enormous amounts of compute and feed it the training data. Weeks or months later, out comes a trained model. Some labs keep their models closed and sell access; others publish the weights for anyone to run.

T10.headline: Serving the model
T10.text: A trained model is just a file until something runs it. Labs and clouds sell access through APIs, inference providers host open-weight models, and serving software makes every chip answer as many requests as it can.

T11.headline: The apps you actually use
T11.text: Chat assistants, coding tools and business apps are built on top of those APIs. This is the end of the chain: the part you see, streaming an answer back token by token.

outro.headline: That's the chain.
outro.text: Tap any box to open it up: who makes it, where, how concentrated it is and what it costs, with a dated source for every number.
